chapter_theme: Paripadal 4, to Tirumal: the praise that cannot add to his fame, his body like gem, sea and cloud, the Prahlada story of the embrace and the claws, his qualities parcelled out among the sun, moon, rain, earth, flower, water, sky and wind, all banners his and the snake-eating eagle decked with snakes, his harshness and grace answering what things hold, and his many places and names, ending with the god as the servant and refuge of each devotee.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god by his form and weapons: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

paripadal:4:1-10.reading: Your devotees, having driven out the five darknesses and wiped clean within the four so that their one thing is guided to you, bow and spread your fame; we know well that our telling is no wonder to you, and that you may fairly laugh at our naming you here and there, yet we speak: your great body is like the sacred gem, the sea whose waves have stilled and the dark womb of the coming rain cloud, your garment is at odds with that dark body, your discus at odds with the lives of those who will not bear you, red-eyed lord without fault.
paripadal:4:1-10.nuance: The counted words of lines 1 and 2 (ஐந்து இருள், நான்கினுள், தம் ஒன்று) are left unexplained by the poem; they read as a discipline of the worshipper (five things cleared away, four cleansed, one left to be guided to the god), not as part of the god's portrait. The double use of முரணிய (lines 8 and 9) sets the gold garment against the dark body and the discus against the god's foes in one figure of contrast.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's deed against the devotee's father, sung as praise: paadaan

paripadal:4:11-24.reading: To praise you, the poet tells how Prahlada, heart smouldering and sandal paste dried, was bound and afflicted with many torments by his father, who scorned you while the son could not scorn you; you embraced the good chest of the one who loved you well and, with the drum roaring like thunder, burst from the broken pillar and with your claws tore again and again the mountain-like chest of the one who would not join you; and your bearing this world and bringing it under your feet is like the much-praised mountain that rises in the middle.
paripadal:4:11-24.nuance: The poem sets the god's two acts on two chests side by side: நன்றா நட்ட அவன் நன் மார்பு முயங்கி (line 16) and ஒன்றா நட்டவன் உறு வரை மார்பின் (line 17); the same hands that embrace the son tear the father. The son is named பிருங்கலாதன் (line 12), a Tamil rendering of Prahlada, and the pillar appears only as ஒடி தூண் (line 20). Lines 22 to 24, on bearing the world, are hard to construe and may refer to another deed.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's qualities found in the elements, sung as praise: paadaan

paripadal:4:25-36.reading: Your heat and brightness are in the sun, your coolness and gentleness in the moon, your pouring and bounty in the rain, your sheltering and endurance in the earth, your fragrance and lustre in the flower, your appearance and breadth in water, your form and sound in the sky, your coming and withdrawing in the wind; so these things here, there and yonder, and all the rest, parted from you who are bound with protection, have come to their fitting places, lord of the high banner of the cock-bird.
paripadal:4:25-36.nuance: The run of eight lines does not say the god is the sun or the moon; it says two of his qualities are found in each (நின் வெம்மையும் விளக்கமும் ஞாயிற்று உள), and line 34 says the things came about by parting from him (நிற் பிரிந்து). The world holds his qualities in pieces, each element two of them. The pairs are chosen to fit their element (sound to the sky, coming and withdrawing to the wind), which matches the order of qualities to elements later counted in the tattva lists.

words: நின் ஒன்றா உயர் கொடி ஒன்று இன்று
thinai_evidence.note: the god's banners and his bird, sung as praise: paadaan

paripadal:4:37-48.reading: Your high banner is the cock-bird; one high banner of yours is the palm, one the plough, one the elephant, and there is no high banner that is not yours; the eagle that crushes the body and life of the venomous snake wears snakes: a snake coiled on its lap, snakes for bangles, on its crown, as its ornament, on its head and on its wings; you who broke the pride of the snake, the one who sits on your banner with green ornaments has the snake for the prey he strikes.
paripadal:4:37-48.nuance: The palm and the plough are the white elder god's marks (Paripadal 1 gives him the plough; Purananuru 56 gives him the palm banner), so the hymn takes the brother's banners as the dark god's own and then says no banner is not his (line 41). The snake passage turns on a paradox: the bird that devours snakes is adorned all over with them, the enemy worn as jewellery.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's nature stated as praise: paadaan

paripadal:4:49-56.reading: Harm that afflicts and fierceness, and favour, cruelty and rightness, heat and coolness: where these are, you have them, and where they are not, you have none; you make no exchange between the lives of those who do not praise you and those who do; the saying that you have neither foes nor kin admits no exception, even when you gain those who praise you; you have no form other than the one the mind takes you to be.
paripadal:4:49-56.nuance: Line 51 (உள்வழி உடையை; இல்வழி இலையே) makes the god's harshness and grace depend on where they are found, not on his preference, and line 56 makes his form the one the worshipper's mind holds (மனக்கோள் நினக்கு என வடிவு). The construal of lines 53 to 55 (மாற்று ஏமாற்றல்; அது போற்றுநர்ப் பெறினே) is doubtful: they may say instead that the god's impartiality yields to those who praise him.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's places and names, sung as praise: paadaan

paripadal:4:57-73.reading: Your body is a choice gem that holds the darkness, you wear a fragrant cluster-garland of opened tulasi, your chest bears the adorned mark that rose from gold; the lotus of ranked petals born from you, the measureless things of lotus-like eyes, your pair of feet that surpass you, the full gods that surpass you, and others besides: in the rare Veda of the brahmins, in the banyan of many branches with leaves like flame and rich shade, in the kadamba, in the middle of the good river, in the hill that stands where no foot goes and elsewhere, you dwell under a different name in each; you are the one in every place, the one who sits at peace in the folded hands of your devotees, the servant of each of them and the refuge of what each does.
paripadal:4:57-73.nuance: Lines 62 and 63 say the god's feet and the full gods surpass the god himself (நின்னின் சிறந்த நின் தாள் இணையவை), so what is worshipped may be ranked above the one it belongs to. The closing lines go further: the god is the servant (ஏவலாளன்) of each worshipper. The sacred places of line 67 and 68 are the banyan, the kadamba, the river islet and the hill, each with its own name for the god.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 10 says he himself is the earth, the sky, the fire, the sun, the moon, the rain and the sea (தானே opening each line); Paripadal 4.25-34 says only that two of the god's qualities are in each of the sun, moon, rain, earth, flower, water, sky and wind, and that these came about by parting from him (நிற் பிரிந்து).
links.teaches: The two lists cover nearly the same things, but the Sangam hymn keeps the god outside them, each element holding a pair of his qualities as a share that left him, while Tirumular erases the gap and makes him the things themselves, so the pair shows identity with the elements was a later and stronger claim than participation.

links.note: Paripadal 1.40-51 says you are the moon, the sun, the sky and the earth; Paripadal 4.25-32 says your coolness is in the moon, your heat in the sun, your form and sound in the sky.
links.teaches: Inside one collection the god is first said to be the moon and the sun and then said to have only lent them his qualities, so the anthology holds both the identity form and the participation form of praise without choosing between them.

links.note: Purananuru 56.1-8 gives four gods four banners: the bull, the palm (பனைக்கொடி) of the conch-white one with the plough, the bird of the sapphire-dark one, the peacock; Paripadal 4.37-41 gives the dark god the bird, the palm, the plough and the elephant, and says there is no banner that is not his. On the plain reading the palm banner belongs to a different god in one poem and to Mal in the other.
links.teaches: The puram poet needs four separate gods so that the king can match each in one excellence, while the devotional poet folds the elder brother's palm and plough into Mal's own emblems, so the pair shows how a hymn's claim of sole lordship rearranged the very iconography the court poets used as a fixed set.

links.note: Paripadal 4.11-21 tells of பிருங்கலாதன் tormented by his father, the god embracing the son and tearing the father's chest with his claws from the broken pillar (ஒடி தூண்); Thiruppugazh 870 tells of a child chanting நம நாராயணாய, the father asking where his god is, and the lion bursting from the pillar to tear Hiranya's chest.
links.teaches: In the Sangam hymn the story turns on the god's two acts on two chests, the embrace and the tearing, while Arunagirinathar's version turns on the child's recitation of the name and the father's challenge, so the pair shows the Prahlada story shifting its centre from the god's protecting hand to the power of the uttered name.

links.note: Kural 4 names God as the one without liking or aversion (வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலான்); Paripadal 4.49-55 says the god has harm and grace, cruelty and rightness wherever these are found and none where they are not, and treats the lives of those who praise him and those who do not without exchange, having neither foes nor kin.
links.teaches: The Kural defines the god by what he lacks, while the hymn shows what that lack allows: he can hold cruelty and grace alike because they answer what is in things rather than his own preference, so freedom from liking and aversion is seen to include, not exclude, the god's harshness.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 3021 asks where he is and answers that the Lord stands everywhere like rain; Paripadal 4.65-70 names the banyan, the kadamba, the river islet and the trackless hill, where he dwells under a different name in each, and concludes எவ் வயினோயும் நீயே, you are the one in every place.
links.teaches: Tirumular reaches omnipresence through the image of rain falling on all places alike, while the Sangam poet reaches it by gathering particular shrines with their own local names, so the pair shows the claim 'he is everywhere' first serving to unite many local cults under one god before it became a claim about space.

links.note: Paripadal 2.20-23 says the god is younger to those who call him younger and elder to those who call him elder; Paripadal 4.69-73 says he bears a different name in each place, sits in the folded hands of his devotees and is the servant (ஏவலாளன்) of each of them.
links.teaches: The rule that the god takes the place each believer gives him begins in Paripadal 2 as a way out of a dispute over rank, and in Paripadal 4 it is extended to names, places and finally to service, so the pair shows accommodation growing from a theological truce into the god's subordinating himself to every worshipper.

source_issues: Paripadal 4: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; only the subject திருமால் is given, and the pan is பாலையாழ், a musical mode, not a thinai.
Paripadal 4 line 25 was flagged as a possible modern heading (heading_dropped), but it is the first of the eight parallel lines 25-32 (நின் வெம்மையும் விளக்கமும் ஞாயிற்று உள) and is verse; kept.

Paripadal 4 lines 8 and 20: lost vowel sign ொ restored in the -ஒடு fault (flags); lines 37 and 40 are not in sangamtamil.com (flag), though line 37 repeats line 36 as a linking refrain and line 40 fits the banner series.
Paripadal 4 line 65 (நின் ஓர் அன்ஓர் அந்தணர் அருமறை) looks corrupt at அன்ஓர், and lines 53-55 and 22-24 are hard to construe; readings there are tentative.
